consolidation

/kun-sol-ih-DAY-shun/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Consolidation means the process of combining several separate things — often companies, offices, or duties — into one stronger, more efficient whole.

The consolidation of the town's three aging libraries into one modern branch doubled the book budget, and after a similar consolidation, the shipping company ran one big warehouse instead of five scattered ones.

Example

The consolidation of the two hospitals' billing departments cut the paperwork in half and ended months of duplicated effort.

Two separate departments become one combined unit that works better and wastes less. That process of merging separate pieces into a single, more efficient whole is a consolidation.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

merger: A merger is the formal event of two or more organizations legally becoming one — the deal itself, announced on a specific day. Consolidation is the broader process of combining overlapping units for strength and efficiency, and it can apply to debts, offices, and duties as well as whole companies.

unification: Unification means bringing separate parts into one, and it usually celebrates the joining itself — the unification of a divided country. Consolidation is more practical bookkeeping than celebration: overlapping units are merged specifically to cut waste and gain strength.

centralization: Centralization gathers decision-making control into one central point while the outlying units themselves can stay where they are. Consolidation actually combines the units: after a consolidation there are fewer offices, not just fewer people in charge.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

fragmentation: breaking apart into pieces

dispersal: a scattering in different directions

Where it sits · how fully the parts become one

combination → consolidation → fusion

combination vs. consolidation: A combination is any joining of things, as casual as mixing two playlists into one — looser than a consolidation, which merges separate parts into one stronger, more efficient whole.

fusion vs. consolidation: A fusion goes further than a consolidation: the separate parts melt together so completely that they can no longer be told apart.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — con-: together, with (Latin)

Root — solid: firm, whole (from Latin solidus)

Suffix — -ation: the action or process of

Put it together: Consolidation is the process (-ation) of making things firm and whole (solidus) together (con-) — pressing separate, wobbly pieces into one solid block.

Use the root in a new word: solidarity: The nurses wore matching pins to show their solidarity during the contract talks.

Root Check

Word Choice

Business / institutional

Consolidation is the go-to word when separate companies, offices, schools, or debts are combined into one stronger, more efficient unit — you'll hear it constantly in business and government news. Compare amalgamation, another word in this unit: an amalgamation blends things of different origins into a brand-new whole, while a consolidation merges similar units mainly for strength and efficiency.
